title: Make everyday cooking part of a calmer household routine
intro: A full-time private chef arrangement in Dubai is most useful when your household needs a consistent cooking presence across a fuller week. That might include more than one meal a day, different preferences within the family or regular guests at home. The aim is a kitchen routine that feels organised and personal. A fuller schedule still needs defined hours, priorities and a practical menu, so this guide explains how to brief the service and keep it aligned with the way your household actually lives.

sections.title: A regular schedule with a defined scope
paragraphs: Full-time describes the planned level of household support; it should not be read as unlimited hours or automatic live-in availability. Discuss the days, meal coverage and responsibilities you need, then review the proposed arrangement in writing.

If you want breakfast, lunch and dinner, explain when each is eaten and who is at home for it. If one meal is usually taken outside, the chef's time may be more useful for preparation or another agreed task. This turns a broad request for a full-time chef into a schedule that can be assessed, priced and delivered realistically.

sections.title: Use a fuller cooking day with clear priorities
paragraphs: A longer chef visit can support more than one meal, but the day still needs a realistic plan. Breakfast preparation, lunch, dinner, grocery tasks and food for later compete for the same hours. Rank what matters most, then discuss which tasks can be combined efficiently and which require dedicated attention.

Meal times can create natural pauses or overlapping demands. If lunch is served while dinner preparation is underway, the chef needs enough workspace and a menu that allows both. If guests are joining in the evening, that may change the daytime priorities or create a need for additional support. A full day should not be treated as unlimited capacity for every kitchen request.

Agree the booked hours and any breaks or scheduling details within the arrangement. Tell myCHEF when the routine changes, especially during school holidays, travel or extended family visits. A fuller household plan works best when it has a clear purpose and can be reviewed against the way the home actually operates.

sections.title: Build one menu around different family appetites
paragraphs: Family cooking works best when the meal feels connected, even if every plate is a little different. A roast, grilled protein or vegetable dish can become the centre of the table, with sauces and sides served separately. This gives people some choice without turning dinner into several unrelated menus that compete for kitchen time.

Tell us about children's usual mealtimes, preferred textures and portion sizes. Some families want familiar dishes throughout the week; others would like gentle introductions to new flavours. Both can be discussed without promising that a particular meal will change anyone's eating habits. For younger children, parents should confirm age-appropriate requirements and any professional advice that needs to be followed.

Think beyond the main meal. You may want a portion set aside for someone arriving late, a lunchbox component or a simple breakfast preparation. These requests should be included in the brief so the chef can plan quantities and priorities rather than fitting extra tasks into an already full visit.

sections.title: Plan arrival time around preparation, not just mealtime
paragraphs: The time you want to eat is different from the time the chef needs to arrive. Ingredients may need preparation, several dishes may need different cooking stages and the table may need attention before guests sit down. Give the team your preferred meal time and ask for an arrival schedule that reflects the agreed menu.

For recurring visits, consider when the kitchen is busiest. Breakfast routines, school departures, deliveries and household staff schedules can all affect access to the workspace. A sensible start time allows the chef to work comfortably while keeping disruption to your household low. If you work from home, mention rooms or periods that need to stay quiet.

Also confirm when the service is expected to finish and what happens if plans run late. Additional tasks or extended service may require more time and an extra charge under the agreed terms. Raising these possibilities before the day is easier than trying to negotiate them while a meal is already underway.

sections.title: Discuss continuity before your routine depends on it
paragraphs: A regular chef can become an important part of the household schedule, so it is sensible to discuss what happens during time off or unexpected unavailability. Tell myCHEF which cooking days are essential and where your routine has some flexibility. That information helps when assessing alternatives.

A replacement needs more than an address. An up-to-date food profile, clear kitchen instructions and a realistic first menu make a handover easier. Keep essential requirements distinct from preferences and flag anything that has changed since the original brief. This is especially useful when several family members eat differently or prepared meals need a particular handover.

A suitable replacement still depends on availability and the requirements of the booking. Avoid building your plans around an unconditional assumption of immediate cover. Ask what options can be offered if the original chef cannot attend and how any proposed change will be confirmed. Clear expectations are more reassuring than a promise that ignores practical limits.

sections.title: Plan household cooking around travel and changing weeks
paragraphs: A recurring chef plan should reflect the weeks when you are actually at home. Tell myCHEF about upcoming travel, visitors and changes to school or work routines as early as possible. These details can affect the most useful menu, the number of portions and the cooking days you want to request.

Before a trip, you may prefer a lighter preparation schedule so food is not left unused. After you return, a well-timed visit can make the first few meals easier. Such changes depend on availability and the terms of your arrangement, so ask for confirmation rather than assuming a visit can always be moved without notice or cost.

Keep your food profile current when guests stay with you. Additional requirements, different mealtimes and a busier kitchen can change the original brief significantly. A short update before the menu is planned gives the chef a better chance to prepare appropriately and keeps the service aligned with the household you have that week.

sections.title: Agree how ingredients reach your kitchen
paragraphs: There are two practical starting points for groceries: have the agreed ingredients ready before the visit, or discuss shopping as part of the service. Either way, the menu needs a clear list. Quantities, preferred brands and acceptable alternatives help avoid delays when an ingredient is unavailable or a household staple has run out.

Keep the service fee and grocery spending easy to understand. Your written proposal should explain who shops, whether shopping time is included in the booked hours and how ingredient costs are handled. If you want a premium cut, specialist imported item or a particular organic product, include that in the brief so it can be priced and sourced appropriately.

It also helps to identify what is already in the kitchen. A quick check of oils, seasonings, rice and other staples can reduce duplicate purchases. For ongoing cooking, agree how the chef should flag low stock and ask before making substitutions that materially change the meal or its cost.

cta.body: Share your date or preferred cooking schedule, Dubai location and the number of people you are planning for. Tell us what you would most like help with, and we will discuss a suitable menu and service arrangement before confirming the details in writing.
